title: DHS Moves to End H-1B Workers' 60-Day Grace Period After Job Loss
excerpt: A proposal to eliminate the safety net that gives laid-off H-1B holders time to find new sponsors has cleared White House review, threatening thousands of Indian professionals.
body:
• The Department of Homeland Security has submitted a proposed rule (RIN 1615-AD22) to the White House Office of Management and Budget that would eliminate the 60-day grace period for H-1B and other employment-based visa holders who lose their jobs.
  • The grace period, in effect since 2017, currently covers H-1B, L-1, O-1, E-1, E-2, E-3, H-1B1, and TN visa holders and their dependents, giving them up to 60 days to find a new employer or change immigration status.
  • Indian nationals accounted for 71% of successful H-1B applicants in fiscal year 2024, making them disproportionately affected by the potential change.
  • The rule has not taken effect and the full regulatory text has not been published; the current 60-day grace period remains in place during the rulemaking process.

What the DHS Is Proposing

The Department of Homeland Security is advancing a proposal that could fundamentally alter the safety net available to foreign workers who lose their jobs in the United States. According to Bloomberg Law, proposed rule RIN 1615-AD22, titled "Eliminating the Discretionary 60-day Grace Period," was submitted to the White House Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs on August 6, 2026, for review.

https://x.com/EricLDaugh/status/2093372374011814331

If finalized, the rule would strip away the 60-day window that currently allows workers in H-1B and several other employment-based visa categories to remain in the country after their sponsored employment ends. Workers and their dependents would generally be required to leave the United States immediately upon losing their jobs, unless U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services exercises discretion to forgive a lapse in status.

"Eliminating the 60-day grace period is both inhumane and unworkable. When a high-skilled worker faces a sudden termination, 60 days is already dangerously short."

— Ajay Jain Bhutoria, former White House adviser

How the Grace Period Works Today

The 60-day grace period was introduced through a 2016 regulation that took effect in January 2017. It applies to workers holding H-1B, H-1B1, L-1, O-1, E-1, E-2, E-3, and TN visas, along with their eligible dependents. During this window, workers can search for a new sponsoring employer, apply to change their immigration status, pursue adjustment of status, or prepare to depart the country.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=nNqp7ciIzwM

According to immigration law firm Ogletree Deakins, individuals are eligible for one 60-day grace period per petition validity period. The clock runs from the date employment ends or until the worker's I-94 record expires, whichever comes first. Before this regulation existed, no such grace period was available.

The provision has proved particularly critical during periods of mass layoffs in the technology sector, where H-1B workers face the dual pressure of job loss and potential deportation on compressed timelines.

Disproportionate Impact on Indian Professionals

Indian nationals stand to bear the heaviest burden if the proposal moves forward. They accounted for 71% of successful H-1B applicants in fiscal year 2024, according to federal data. The Indian-American population in the United States is estimated at approximately 5.2 million.

For many H-1B professionals, a layoff triggers a cascade of consequences beyond unemployment — immigration status, family stability, housing obligations, children's schooling, and career prospects all hang in the balance. The grace period has served as a buffer, giving workers and their families time to make decisions without immediately falling out of legal status.

Immigration attorney Richard T. Herman, writing in HR Executive, noted that the change would disproportionately affect smaller employers. "A start-up, hospital, university or midsize manufacturer may discover a strong candidate on day 30 and spend the next two weeks determining whether sponsorship is possible," he wrote. "A shorter clock rewards the employer with the fastest paperwork — not necessarily the best job or strongest use for the worker's skills."

What Comes Next

The proposal must clear several steps before it can take effect. Once the Office of Management and Budget completes its review, the proposed rule will be published in the Federal Register and opened for public comment, typically for 30 to 60 days. After the comment period, DHS could withdraw, modify, or finalize the rule. If it proceeds to final rulemaking, it would likely take several additional months before implementation.

Ogletree Deakins noted there is a possibility the agency may abandon the proposal entirely based on public feedback. The current 60-day grace period remains fully in effect throughout the rulemaking process.

The development is part of a broader set of proposed policy changes affecting the H-1B program under the Trump administration, including a proposed $103,000 fee for H-1B cap-subject petitions and tighter scrutiny of Optional Practical Training for international students. For H-1B workers already navigating an uncertain job market, the stakes of this regulatory process could not be higher.
nri_angle: Directly threatens hundreds of thousands of Indian H-1B workers in the US who could face immediate deportation after job loss without the current 60-day buffer.
